body:
# Background

Section V13.2 only has one requirement left. I propose merging it into V13.1.


# Current State

## V13.1 Generic Web Service Security

This section promotes generic web service security considerations and consequently basic web service hygiene practices in general.

| # | Description | Level | CWE |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: |
| **13.1.1** | [MOVED TO 5.5.5] | | |
| **13.1.2** | [DELETED] | | |
| **13.1.3** | [DELETED, MERGED TO 8.1.11] | | |
| **13.1.4** | [DELETED, COVERED BY 4.1.6] | | |
| **13.1.5** | [DELETED, INSUFFICIENT IMPACT] | | |
| **13.1.6** | [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 13.2.6, COVERS 13.3.2, LEVEL L2 > L3] Verify that per-message digital signatures are used to provide additional assurance on top of transport protections for requests or transactions which are highly sensitive or which traverse a number of systems. | 3 | 345 |
| **13.1.7** | [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 14.4.1, COVERS 5.3.2] Verify that every HTTP response with a message body contains a Content-Type header field that matches the actual content of the response, including the charset parameter to specify safe character encoding (e.g., UTF-8, ISO-8859-1) according to IANA Media Types, such as "text/", "/+xml" and "/xml". | 1 | 173 |
| **13.1.8** | [ADDED] Verify that only user-facing endpoints (intended for manual web-browser access) automatically redirect from HTTP to HTTPS, while other services or endpoints do not implement transparent redirects. This is to avoid a situation where a client is erroneously sending unencrypted HTTP requests but, since the requests are being automatically redirected to HTTPS, the leakage of sensitive data goes undiscovered. | 2 | |

## V13.2 Web Services

As at this time, there is a "published version" of the JSON schema validation specification, which is considered production ready. However, there is not yet a version which is considered strictly "stable". As such, when considering using JSON schema validation, be sure to also apply the standard input validation guidance from Chapter 5 of ASVS.

Due to the lack of a formal stable version of the JSON schema validation specification, carefully monitor any JSON schema validation libraries in use, as they may need to be updated once the standard is formalized and bugs are ironed out of reference implementations.

Note: Due to issues with XXE attacks against DTDs, DTD validation should not be used, and framework DTD evaluation disabled as per the requirements set out in chapter V5.

This could involve implementing schema validation for formats like JSON and XML. | 3 | 20 |

# Proposal

See: #2665

comments.body: Validation for 13.2.2 - is my application less secure if I don't meet this requirement?
It is basically advanced input validation. It is very hard to do but then it is also L3.
It does not answer to my question :)

We see input validation as an important control, this is a way of implementing comprehensive input validation. If we think that 11.3.1 is important (for all input as defined at L2), then presumably this requirement is also important. Maybe this requirement theoretically duplicates 11.3.1 but I think it would be more accurate to say that it provides an elegant way to achieve it.

> We see input validation as an important control, this is a way of implementing comprehensive input validation. If we think that 11.3.1 is important (for all input as defined at L2), then presumably this requirement is also important

No, it is different from 11.3.1 - 11.3.1 requires input validation for the data items that are used by the application.

13.2.2 requires to validate to "container" or the "package" format for all those input delivered to the application and at the same time says, that all those inputs need to be validated separately (that means requirement 11.3.1).

Entire section text for V13.2 are disclaimers that JSON schema contains this and that risks and DTD should not be used. So, what precise security problem it solves that is not already addressed by 11.3.1, 5.5.*?

> 13.2.2 requires to validate to "container" or the "package" format for all those input delivered to the application and at the same time says, that all those inputs need to be validated separately (that means requirement 11.3.1).

JSON/XML schema validation verifies that the _**complete data structure adheres to an expected contract**_. This means that before you even get to validating individual fields, you ensure the whole object is well-structured. This is something that you cannot do with 11.3.1.

Again, when you enforce an overall schema, the system can _**quickly reject the entire request**_ if it does not conform to the expected structure, before you even bother doing data validation of each individual item. This reduces the risk of processing data that can cause logic errors or similar.

Schema validation also ensures that only correctly formatted JSON is being parsed, which minimizes attacks on the parser itself, as a secondary benefit. Even if 5.5.x covers the general requirements of deserialization problems in libraries, it's schema validation that helps support this. And again, IMO, this is just a secondary benefit.

13.2.2 is solid in my opinion and is fairly fundamental to secure software. 

PS: JSON Schema validation, Draft‑07, is a well-tested and broadly supported option. It's incredibly stable and has been around for 5 or so years.

I can understand the abstract benefit, but I'm not convinced it is impactful enough to be worth a requirement.

For validation we may use questions like:
* What is the security problem to solve?
* Is it practical and realistic?
  * Effort to implement vs security benefits to get
  * Is it valuable or ignored when reported in a report?

If to keep it, I don't think it fits to general web service requirement. It can be also in input validation, defensive coding, or File Integrity and Content.

> I can understand the abstract benefit, but I'm not convinced it is impactful enough to be worth a requirement.

I think that’s a very fair perspective Elar. I’m trying to keep it in because I really think it’s a very good developer security behavior to do schema validation -  in general. But I agree it’s more of an abstract than a specific benefit.

If you’re OK with keeping it, then I feel comfortable moving it as you suggested. But I think your concerns here are very fair.

Having discussed with @elarlang, it feels like this requirement is not exactly a security requirement in itself but rather just a way to achieve input validation which we cover else where anyway.

11.3.1 is talking about input validation individually but it could also be achieved using this mechanism as well.

What do you think @jmanico ?
I stand by https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2664#issuecomment-2698746939 but respect your decisions.

Yeah, the more I think about it the more I see it as a mechanism rather than a requirement, 

@elarlang what do you think about the updates in the PR, with particular consideration of the "COVERS" tag
